This notebook visualizes the cohort-pooling simulation produced by
`Coding/Paper1_Submission2/cohort_pooling_simulation.R`. The simulation makes
the rebuttal to the "your cohorts are contrived by construction" critique
concrete: an exposure-outcome association is a property of the **unit** (cohort
/ location) it emerged from, and naively pooling across units can blur or even
reverse the signal that is real within each unit (Simpson's paradox /
ecological-aggregation bias). This is the cross-sectional analog of the
longitudinal *within-person vs. between-person* decomposition, with **cohort**
in the role of subject.

Two regimes are shown:

- **Averaging** -- effects are genuinely heterogeneous across cohorts (with no
  cross-cohort confounding by construction); pooling is honest on average -- the
  pooled estimate lands on the within-cohort effect -- but it collapses the
  heterogeneity into a single number that represents no real location.
- **Simpson** -- the effect is positive within *every* cohort, yet naive pooling
  returns a *negative* association because high-exposure locations happen to
  have lower baseline outcomes.

## Input Files

```{r}
resolve_existing_path <- function(candidates) {
  existing <- candidates[file.exists(candidates)]
  if (length(existing) == 0) {
    stop(
      "Could not find the pooling simulation output directory. Checked:\n",
      paste(candidates, collapse = "\n")
    )
  }
  existing[[1]]
}

sim_dir <- dirname(resolve_existing_path(c(
  "../../../Output/Paper1_Output_Submission2/Pooling_Sim_Output/pooling_sim_estimands.csv",
  "../../Output/Paper1_Output_Submission2/Pooling_Sim_Output/pooling_sim_estimands.csv",
  "Output/Paper1_Output_Submission2/Pooling_Sim_Output/pooling_sim_estimands.csv"
)))

individual <- readr::read_csv(file.path(sim_dir, "pooling_sim_individual.csv"),
                              show_col_types = FALSE)
per_cohort <- readr::read_csv(file.path(sim_dir, "pooling_sim_per_cohort.csv"),
                              show_col_types = FALSE)
estimands  <- readr::read_csv(file.path(sim_dir, "pooling_sim_estimands.csv"),
                              show_col_types = FALSE)
curve      <- readr::read_csv(file.path(sim_dir, "pooling_sim_curve.csv"),
                              show_col_types = FALSE)
sim_params <- readr::read_csv(file.path(sim_dir, "pooling_sim_params.csv"),
                              show_col_types = FALSE)
budget        <- readr::read_csv(file.path(sim_dir, "budget_allocation_results.csv"),
                                 show_col_types = FALSE)
budget_params <- readr::read_csv(file.path(sim_dir, "budget_allocation_params.csv"),
                                 show_col_types = FALSE)

# Real ExWAS diagnostic (sibling output folder)
diag_dir <- file.path(dirname(sim_dir), "Cohort_Regime_Diagnostic")
diag_pairs    <- readr::read_csv(file.path(diag_dir, "cohort_regime_pairs.csv"),
                                 show_col_types = FALSE)
diag_coverage <- readr::read_csv(file.path(diag_dir, "cohort_regime_coverage_summary.csv"),
                                 show_col_types = FALSE)

regime_levels <- c("averaging", "simpson")
regime_labels <- c(averaging = "Averaging", simpson = "Simpson")

prettify_regime <- function(x) {
  factor(recode(x, !!!regime_labels), levels = unname(regime_labels))
}

individual <- individual %>%
  mutate(regime = prettify_regime(regime), cohort = factor(cohort))
per_cohort <- per_cohort %>%
  mutate(regime = prettify_regime(regime), cohort = factor(cohort))
estimands  <- estimands  %>% mutate(regime = prettify_regime(regime))
curve      <- curve      %>% mutate(regime = prettify_regime(regime))
```

```{r}
regime_palette <- c(
  "Averaging" = "#0F4C5C",
  "Simpson"   = "#D17A22"
)

estimand_palette <- c(
  "Within-cohort (contextual)" = "#0F4C5C",
  "Naive pooled"               = "#D17A22",
  "Between-cohort (ecological)" = "#9A4C95"
)

pooling_theme <- function() {
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15, color = "#14213D"),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10.5, color = "#4F5D75"),
      axis.title = element_text(face = "bold", color = "#14213D"),
      axis.text = element_text(color = "#2B2D42"),
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", color = "#14213D"),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "#E6E8EF", linewidth = 0.3),
      panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "#D9DEE8", linewidth = 0.35),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      legend.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
      legend.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA)
    )
}

# Long-format estimand table for plotting / tabulating the three summaries.
estimand_long <- estimands %>%
  select(regime,
         `Within-cohort (contextual)` = within_adjusted,
         `Naive pooled` = naive_pooled,
         `Between-cohort (ecological)` = between_cohort) %>%
  pivot_longer(-regime, names_to = "estimand", values_to = "beta") %>%
  mutate(estimand = factor(estimand, levels = names(estimand_palette)))

# Budget-allocation metrics in long form. Two goals want MANY diverse units
# (their error falls with K); one wants ENOUGH per unit (its error rises with K).
budget_metric_levels <- c(
  "Population-average effect (RMSE)"   = "beta_within_rmse",
  "Cross-cohort heterogeneity (RMSE)"  = "tau_rmse",
  "Single location (median SE)"        = "median_location_se"
)
budget_palette <- c(
  "Population-average effect (RMSE)"  = "#0F4C5C",
  "Cross-cohort heterogeneity (RMSE)" = "#9A4C95",
  "Single location (median SE)"       = "#D17A22"
)

budget_long <- budget %>%
  select(K, n_per, all_of(unname(budget_metric_levels))) %>%
  pivot_longer(-c(K, n_per), names_to = "metric_key", values_to = "value") %>%
  mutate(metric = factor(
    names(budget_metric_levels)[match(metric_key, budget_metric_levels)],
    levels = names(budget_metric_levels)
  ))
```

## Estimand Summary

The headline table: within each regime, the three ways of estimating "the
association" diverge. `within_true` is the data-generating contextual effect;
`within_adjusted` recovers it; `naive_pooled` does not.

```{r}
estimands %>%
  select(regime, within_true, within_adjusted, naive_pooled, between_cohort) %>%
  kable(digits = 3,
        col.names = c("Regime", "Within (true)", "Within (adjusted)",
                      "Naive pooled", "Between (ecological)"))
```

```{r}
per_cohort %>%
  group_by(regime) %>%
  summarise(
    cohorts = n(),
    min_beta_hat = min(beta_hat),
    median_beta_hat = median(beta_hat),
    max_beta_hat = max(beta_hat),
    frac_negative = mean(beta_hat < 0),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  kable(digits = 3,
        col.names = c("Regime", "Cohorts", "Min beta", "Median beta",
                      "Max beta", "Frac. negative"))
```

## Plot 1: Within-Cohort vs Naive Pooled Fits

The clearest single picture. Colored lines are within-cohort fits; the heavy
black line is the single naive pooled fit. In the Simpson regime the pooled
line slopes the *opposite* way to every cohort it is built from.

> **How to read this panel (the basis for patchplot A).**
>
> *What is plotted.* Each point is one subject; **X** is exposure, **Y** is the
> outcome. Points are colored by cohort, so each colored cloud is a single
> location's data. The **thin colored line** through each cloud is that
> location's own fit (`lm(y ~ x)` within the cohort) -- the *contextual* effect.
> The **heavy dark line** is the single naive pooled fit (`lm(y ~ x)` on
> everyone at once, ignoring the cohort label).
>
> *Averaging regime.* The colored clouds sit at different exposure levels and
> their slopes genuinely disagree -- some tilt up, some flat, a few down. The
> dark pooled line runs through the middle of them: it is roughly the **average**
> of the cohort slopes. It is not "wrong" -- pooling is honest on average here --
> but it represents no actual location and it **hides the disagreement** that is
> plainly visible in the colored lines.
>
> *Simpson regime.* Every colored cloud tilts **upward** (positive within each
> location), yet the clouds are arranged so that higher-exposure locations sit
> **lower** on the Y axis. The dark pooled line follows that downward staircase
> across clouds and ends up tilting **down** -- the opposite sign of every
> cohort it was built from. Ignoring the cohort unit has not blurred the signal,
> it has **reversed** it.
>
> *Takeaway.* The line that answers the science is the within-cohort one. The
> pooled line can disagree with all of its parts.

```{r fig.width=11, fig.height=5.5}
p_within_vs_pooled <- individual %>%
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = cohort), alpha = 0.18, size = 0.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_smooth(aes(color = cohort, group = cohort), method = "lm", se = FALSE,
              linewidth = 0.45, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#14213D", linewidth = 1.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ regime, scales = "free") +
  scale_color_manual(values = colorRampPalette(
    as.character(paletteer::paletteer_d("ggsci::springfield_simpsons")))(
      n_distinct(individual$cohort))) +
  labs(
    title = "Within-Cohort Fits vs the Naive Pooled Fit",
    subtitle = "Dark line = pooled lm(y ~ x); thin lines = per-cohort fits. Simpson regime: pooled slope reverses sign.",
    x = "Exposure (X)",
    y = "Outcome (Y)"
  ) +
  pooling_theme()

p_within_vs_pooled
```

```{r fig.width=11, fig.height=5}
  ggplot(aes(x = beta_hat)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 16, fill = "#C9D2DF", color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +

  labs(
    title = "Per-Cohort Exposure Effects and the Pooled Summaries",

    x = "Estimated exposure effect",
    y = "Number of cohorts",
    color = NULL
  ) +
  pooling_theme()

p_cohort_hist
```

## Plot 3: Pooling Toward the Limit

As the sampling unit grows from 1 to all K cohorts, the naive pooled estimate
converges to its population limit. The dashed red line is the within-cohort
(contextual) effect: in the Averaging regime the limit lands *on* it (only the
heterogeneity is lost), while in the Simpson regime it converges *away* from it.

> **How to read this panel (the basis for patchplot B).**
>
> *What is plotted.* The **X axis** is `m`, the number of cohorts pooled
> together, from 1 up to all of them. The **Y axis** is the **naive pooled
> effect** -- the slope from `lm(y ~ x)` when those `m` cohorts are combined and
> the cohort label is ignored. For each `m`, we draw many random subsets of `m`
> cohorts, fit the pooled model on each, and summarize: the **black line** is the
> average slope and the **grey band** is its 5th-95th percentile (how much the
> answer depends on *which* cohorts you happened to pool). The **dashed red
> line** is the within-cohort (contextual) truth -- flat, because it does not
> depend on how many cohorts you pool.
>
> *The sweep is the point.* Moving left to right walks from a single-unit
> finding (`m = 1`, the "n = 1" analog) toward the population limit (`m` = all
> cohorts). This is the cross-sectional version of the longitudinal
> *one subject -> population* trajectory, with cohort as the unit.
>
> *Reading the ends.* At the **left** the band is wide (with one cohort you are
> at the mercy of which one you drew) but the line sits near the truth. At the
> **right** the band **collapses to almost a point** -- pool everything and there
> is no sampling randomness left. Where it collapses to is the whole story:
>
> - **Averaging regime:** the line stays **on** the dashed red truth as `m`
>   grows; only the band shrinks. Pooling is honest on average -- but the
>   cohort-to-cohort heterogeneity that was visible at `m = 1` is **averaged
>   away** by the limit.
> - **Simpson regime:** the line starts positive, then **bends down across zero**
>   and converges *away* from the red truth. Adding cohorts does not fix the
>   bias; it accumulates it. The tight band at the limit is the trap -- a
>   precise-looking estimate with the **wrong sign**.
>
> *Takeaway.* More data (a larger pooled sample) shrinks the **variance** of the
> naive estimate but does nothing for its **cohort-driven bias**. "Bigger pool =
> more trustworthy" is only true for uncertainty, not for the bias, so the
> within-cohort analysis is not optional at any sample size.

```{r fig.width=11, fig.height=5}
within_ref <- estimands %>% select(regime, within = within_adjusted)

p_limit <- curve %>%
  ggplot(aes(m, mean_slope)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), alpha = 0.18, fill = "#0F4C5C") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.95, color = "#14213D") +
  geom_hline(data = within_ref, aes(yintercept = within),
             linetype = "dashed", color = "#C1121F", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "#9AA3AD", linewidth = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ regime, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "As the Sampling Unit Approaches the Limit",
    subtitle = "Naive pooled effect vs number of cohorts pooled. Dashed red = within-cohort effect; band = 5-95% over random subsets.",
    x = "Number of cohorts pooled (m)",
    y = "Naive pooled exposure effect"
  ) +
  pooling_theme()

p_limit
```

## Plot 4: Exposure Profiles Differ Across Locations

The mechanism behind the paradox: each location occupies a different stretch of
the exposure axis. Pooling stitches these offset clouds together, and the
between-location trend can dominate the within-location signal.

```{r fig.width=11, fig.height=5}
p_profiles <- individual %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = x, fill = regime)) +
  geom_density(aes(group = cohort), color = NA, alpha = 0.25) +
  facet_wrap(~ regime, scales = "free") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = regime_palette, guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Cohort-Specific Exposure Profiles",
    subtitle = "Each density is one location's exposure distribution",
    x = "Exposure (X)",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  pooling_theme()

p_profiles
```

## Plot 5: Budget Allocation -- Diverse Units vs Unplanned Volume

This panel answers the design question behind the rebuttal: given a **fixed
budget** (total sample size held constant), how should you spend it? We sweep
the allocation from a few large cohorts to many small cohorts -- `K` cohorts of
`n_per` each with `K * n_per` constant -- and track three things you might want
from the study. It is produced by
`Coding/Paper1_Submission2/budget_allocation_simulation.R`.

> **How to read this panel.**
>
> *X axis:* number of cohorts `K` (log scale), with the subjects-per-cohort it
> implies printed underneath -- moving right means *more, smaller* cohorts for
> the same total budget. *Y axis:* error / uncertainty (lower is better).
>
> - **Population-average effect (teal)** and **cross-cohort heterogeneity
>   (purple)** both **fall** as you add units. With only a few large cohorts you
>   have a big sample but the *handful of contexts you sampled* cannot represent
>   the population of locations -- the error here scales with the number of
>   **units** (~ `tau / sqrt(K)`), not the number of people. Piling more
>   subjects into a few convenient sites does **not** fix it.
> - **Single location (orange)** moves the other way: it **rises** as cohorts
>   shrink, because each location is estimated from fewer subjects. Push to many
>   tiny cohorts and any one location's estimate becomes noise.
>
> *Takeaway.* The two curves form a scissors. There is no single-number "best,"
> but the defensible region is the middle -- a **deliberately diverse set of
> locations, each with enough subjects** -- not "as small as possible" and not
> "everyone from a few unplanned, convenient sites." The left edge is exactly
> the design the reviewer's critique would push you toward; this panel shows what
> it costs.

```{r}
budget %>%
  transmute(
    `Cohorts (K)` = K,
    `Subjects / cohort` = n_per,
    `Pop. effect RMSE` = beta_within_rmse,
    `Heterogeneity RMSE` = tau_rmse,
    `Single-location SE` = median_location_se
  ) %>%
  kable(digits = 3)
```

```{r fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
k_breaks <- sort(unique(budget$K))
k_labels <- budget %>%
  distinct(K, n_per) %>%
  arrange(K) %>%
  mutate(lab = glue("{K}\n({n_per})")) %>%
  pull(lab)

p_budget <- budget_long %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = K, y = value, color = metric)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.05) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = k_breaks, labels = k_labels) +
  scale_color_manual(values = budget_palette) +
  labs(
    title = "Spending a Fixed Budget: Diverse Units vs Unplanned Volume",
    subtitle = "Total N held constant. Two goals want many diverse units (falling); one wants enough subjects per unit (rising).",
    x = "Number of cohorts  (subjects per cohort)",
    y = "Error / uncertainty (lower is better)",
    color = NULL
  ) +
  pooling_theme() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8))

# Shown inline only; the budget panel is exported as panel C of the
# Cohort_Pooling_Simulation_Patchplot, so no standalone PDF is written.
p_budget
```

## Real ExWAS: What Is Actually Happening

The simulation shows what *can* happen when associations are pooled across
cohorts. This panel shows what *does* happen in the targeted ExWAS. Of the
thousands of exposure-outcome pairs, the overwhelming majority are observed in
a **single cohort** (see coverage below), so pooling is not even possible. Only
the handful of pairs seen in **>= 3 cohorts** can be examined for the pooling
phenomenon -- and that is exactly the set shown here.

```{r}
diag_coverage %>%
  transmute(
    Panel = recode(panel, child = "Child", mat = "Maternal"),
    `Pairs (total)` = pairs_total,
    `1 cohort` = pairs_1_cohort,
    `>=2 cohorts` = pairs_ge2_cohort,
    `>=3 cohorts` = pairs_ge3_cohort,
    `% single-cohort` = pct_single_cohort
  ) %>%
  kable()
```

The combined real-data figure below pulls together three views on the
**maternal** panel, the same slice as the manuscript heterogeneity figure:

- **A -- cohorts disagree by location.** Per-cohort adjusted effect estimates
  (z-statistics) for each exposure|outcome, colored by study location; 67% of
  exposures have cohorts on both sides of zero.
- **B -- pooling distorts the contextual effect.** For the **same pairs as A**,
  the within-cohort (filled) vs naive-pooled (open) standardized effect; the
  connecting segment is the distortion from pooling, and a crossing of zero
  (red) is Simpson's paradox. (Unadjusted decomposition: it isolates the
  cohort-pooling mechanism, and full covariate adjustment is infeasible here
  because covariate completeness is itself cohort-specific.)
- **C -- heterogeneity is not just an exposure-range artifact.** I^2 versus the
  between-cohort concentration fold-change shows no clear relationship
  (Spearman rho ~ 0.24).

The figure is built by `Vis_Code/combined_realdata_figure.R` (which also writes
`Final_Patchplots/MS_Fig_RealData_Combined.pdf`); we source it here so it renders
right after the simulation figure.

```{r fig.width=9, fig.height=17}
source("combined_realdata_figure.R")
combined
```

The real data matches the simulation's warning: where pooling *is* possible
(panel B), the naive pooled effect (open) routinely sits away from the
within-cohort effect (filled), pulled toward the ecological slope (diamond) --
mostly inflating the magnitude, occasionally flipping the sign. But such pairs
are the rare exception; for almost the entire ExWAS there is only one cohort per
pair (coverage table above), which is itself the strongest argument for
analyzing associations within their cohort unit rather than pooling across
contrived cohort differences.
